\chapter{Five More Everyday Actions}
\label{ch:aprender-y-cocinar}
\hlchaptermodality{396}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say aprender, cocinar, preferir, funcionar and reparar, and name five everyday actions.}

Complete ES-C396-reparar: name five everyday actions, and say one thing about each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[aprender]{aprender — the hand closes on it}

\label{lesson:ES-C396-aprender}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to lose}, then \emph{to need}. (\emph{Perder}; \emph{necesitar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item estudiar — the work you put in.
  \item la escuela — the building it happens in.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-pren-DER}, three beats with the weight on the last. The \emph{pr} runs together with nothing between the two letters, and each \emph{r} is a light tap of the tongue rather than the English glide. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{aprender} — \textquotedblleft{}to learn.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{apprehendere} meant to seize: \emph{ad-}, toward, plus \textbf{prehendere}, to grasp. Speech wore it down long before Spanish existed — the \emph{-he-} in the middle fell out, leaving \textbf{apprēndere}, and the doubled \emph{pp} thinned to one. Those two small losses are the fingerprints of a word that came down a road.

Then Latin handed Spanish the very same verb a second time, copied off a page this time, and the copy landed intact: \textbf{aprehender}. Its \emph{-he-} is still sitting there, and that untouched cluster is what tells you which route the word took.

Two arrivals, two jobs, and swapping them is a real error. Police \textbf{aprehenden} a suspect. Students \textbf{aprenden} a language. The bookish twin kept the seizing; the worn one kept only the metaphor.

And that metaphor is worth defending, because it is not guesswork. Medieval Latin already had the verb meaning to learn — the sense is written down, not inferred from the root by someone who liked the picture. English carries that very sense in \textbf{apprentice}, a person who takes hold of a trade.

The plainer English relatives keep the grip: \textbf{apprehend}, to seize a person or a meaning; \textbf{comprehend}, to take hold of something whole; \textbf{prehensile}, of a tail that grasps a branch; and \textbf{prey}, the thing seized.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{aprender}. And you can read a preserved \emph{-he-} as a sign that a word arrived off a page rather than down a road.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{aprender}
  \item \emph{necesito aprender}
  \item \emph{aprender en la escuela}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{apprehendere} mean in Latin? (To seize, to grasp.) Which of \emph{aprender} and \emph{aprehender} would a police report reach for, and what marks it as the copy off the page? (\emph{Aprehender} — it kept the \emph{-he-} whole, and it kept the seizing.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cocinar]{cocinar — one Latin word, two kitchens}

\label{lesson:ES-C396-cocinar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to need}, then \emph{to learn}. (\emph{Necesitar}; \emph{aprender}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la comida — what comes out of it.
  \item la casa — where the room is.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{co-ci-NAR}, three beats with the weight on the last. One word, both values of the letter \emph{c}: a hard \emph{k} in front of the \emph{o}, and in front of the \emph{i} a soft one — an \emph{s} across the Americas, a \emph{th} across much of Spain. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{cocinar} — \textquotedblleft{}to cook.\textquotedblright{}

The verb is young and the room is old. Underneath it sits \textbf{cocina}, the kitchen, which is Latin \textbf{coquīna}, from \textbf{coquere}, to cook. Corominas finds \emph{cocina} in Spanish by the year 947 and puts no mark against it — no suggestion it was lifted out of a book. It came down by mouth, like the food.

The \emph{qu} of \emph{coquīna} had a \emph{w}-colour in it, and Latin lost that colour in front of a back vowel. What is left is the plain \emph{c} of \emph{cocina}.

Now the fact worth carrying away. English \textbf{kitchen} is that same Latin noun. Germanic speakers borrowed it early, out of an everyday Latin form reconstructed as \emph{cocina}, and Old English wrote it \textbf{cycene}; English mouths turned that into \emph{kitchen}. Spanish, meanwhile, kept the room close to its Latin shape. Two peoples took one word in opposite directions and neither can hear the other in it. \textbf{Cook} is the same family — Old English \emph{coc}, from Latin \textbf{coquus} — and \textbf{cuisine} is the same room once more, come round by way of French.

One caution about the verb, and one about the neighbours.

\textbf{Cocer} and \textbf{cocinar} are not swaps for one another. \emph{Cocer} is the old inherited verb for a particular process, boiling or baking a thing. \emph{Cocinar} is the newer one built on the room, and it covers the whole activity.

And \emph{coco}, \emph{cocaína} and \emph{cochino} have nothing to do with any of this. They merely start the same way.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{cocinar}. And you know one Latin noun that reached English and Spanish by separate roads and surfaced as \emph{kitchen} in one and \emph{cocina} in the other.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cocinar}
  \item \emph{aprender a cocinar}
  \item \emph{necesito cocinar hoy}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which English word is \emph{cocina} in other clothes? (\emph{Kitchen} — Old English \emph{cycene}, borrowed early from Vulgar Latin.) And which of \emph{cocer} and \emph{cocinar} names the general activity? (\emph{Cocinar}; \emph{cocer} names a process, boiling or baking.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[preferir]{preferir — a verb Spanish never inherited}

\label{lesson:ES-C396-preferir}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to learn}, then \emph{to cook}. (\emph{Aprender}; \emph{cocinar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item gustar — the neighbour that says what pleases you.
  \item elegir — the neighbour that acts on it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pre-fe-RIR}, three beats with the weight on the last. The \emph{pr} runs together with nothing between the letters, and each \emph{r} is a light tap. Said of yourself, the middle beat comes out differently: \emph{pre-FYE-ro}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{preferir} — \textquotedblleft{}to prefer.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{praeferre} is \emph{prae-}, in front, plus \textbf{ferre}, to carry. To carry one thing in front of another is to put it first, and putting a thing first is what preferring has been ever since.

This verb came out of a book, and for once the evidence is airtight. Latin \emph{ferre} was irregular — one of the ragged verbs every Latin student meets — and Spanish inherited nothing from it. Not one verb. Yet Spanish has a shelf of them: \emph{preferir}, \emph{referir}, \emph{transferir}, \emph{conferir}, \emph{diferir}. A family with no ancestor in the language is a family of imports, and the tell is that they arrived as a set and were all handed to the same \emph{-ir} class on the way in. \emph{Preferir} is first documented in 1490, in Alfonso de Palencia.

Now set its forms side by side and watch the middle beat:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{preferir} — the bare verb;
  \item \textbf{prefiero} — what I do;
  \item \textbf{prefieres} — what you do.
\end{itemize}

That \emph{e} turning into \emph{ie} is worth a thought rather than a label. An inherited sound change is out of the question here: it would have run its course centuries before 1490, and there was no Spanish \emph{ferre} for it to run on. The \emph{ie} must have come from somewhere else — most plausibly the newcomer falling in with native verbs already built that way, \emph{sentir} and \emph{siento} among them. That is reasoning, though, not a finding: no source consulted here states it. Hold it loosely.

The English relatives are \textbf{prefer} and \textbf{preference}. Behind them, \emph{ferre} is the same ancient root as English \textbf{bear}, which is why \textbf{refer}, \textbf{transfer}, \textbf{differ}, \textbf{suffer} and \textbf{fertile} belong to the household.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say what you prefer: \emph{preferir}. And you can treat a whole set of verbs landing together in one class as evidence of where they came from.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{preferir}
  \item \emph{prefiero cocinar}
  \item \emph{prefiero aprender en casa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is \emph{preferir} certain to be a borrowing? (Latin \emph{ferre} left Spanish no inherited verb at all, and the whole \emph{-ferir} set arrived together in one class.) And is the \emph{ie} of \emph{prefiero} an inherited sound change? (No — and the account offered here, falling in with \emph{sentir} and \emph{siento}, is reasoning rather than a finding.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[funcionar]{funcionar — the machine works, the doctor does not}

\label{lesson:ES-C396-funcionar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to cook}, then \emph{to prefer}. (\emph{Cocinar}; \emph{preferir}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el teléfono — a thing that does this or fails to.
  \item trabajar — the word for people, kept separate.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{fun-cio-NAR}, three beats with the weight on the last. The \emph{cio} is one glide and not two beats: a soft \emph{c} before the \emph{i}, then straight out into the \emph{o}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{funcionar} — \textquotedblleft{}to work,\textquotedblright{} said of a thing rather than a person.

Underneath it is \textbf{función}, and under that Latin \textbf{fūnctiō}, accusative \textbf{fūnctiōnem} — a carrying-out, the discharging of a duty — from the verb \textbf{fungī}, to perform. A Roman's \emph{fūnctiō} was an office done properly. A Spanish machine's \emph{función} is the job it exists to do, and \emph{funcionar} is that job actually getting done.

Look at the \emph{-ct-} that Latin wrote in the middle of \emph{fūnctiōnem}, because it is a passport stamp. Latin clusters of that shape, carried down by mouth, come out of Spanish as \emph{ch}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{factum} $\to$ \textbf{hecho};
  \item \emph{noctem} $\to$ \textbf{noche}.
\end{itemize}

Had \emph{fūnctiōnem} walked that same road, Spanish would be saying something like \emph{fuchón} today. It says \emph{función}. The cluster survived because the word never made the journey — it was copied out of written Latin long after the mouths had finished their work.

One claim to hold at arm's length. You will meet the assertion that \emph{funcionar} came into Spanish from French \emph{fonctionner}, a nineteenth-century import. It may have. Neither route consulted for this lesson mentions French at all, and nothing here could test it, so it stays a claim rather than a fact. French mediation \emph{is} documented for the English word — but that is a different language's history, and it settles nothing about this one.

The trap is a live one. \textbf{El coche funciona} — the car works. \textbf{El médico trabaja} — the doctor works. \emph{El médico funciona} is wrong, and English hides the difference by using one verb for both.

English holds the same Latin in \textbf{function}, in \textbf{defunct}, and in \textbf{perfunctory}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say that a thing works: \emph{funcionar}. And you can read an untouched Latin cluster as proof that a word came off a page.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{funcionar}
  \item \emph{el teléfono funciona}
  \item \emph{prefiero cocinar en casa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What would \emph{fūnctiōnem} look like had it come down by mouth? (Something like \emph{fuchón} — that cluster gives \emph{ch}, as in \emph{hecho} and \emph{noche}.) And can you say \emph{el médico funciona}? (No. A machine \emph{funciona}; a person \emph{trabaja}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[reparar]{reparar — the word that cannot say where it has been}

\label{lesson:ES-C396-reparar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to prefer}, then \emph{to work}, of a machine. (\emph{Preferir}; \emph{funcionar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item romper — what happens first.
  \item la harina — a word whose sounds do name its road.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{re-pa-RAR}, three beats with the weight on the last. The opening \emph{r} is a full roll; the two inside are light taps. The \emph{p} carries no puff of air. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{reparar} — \textquotedblleft{}to repair.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{reparāre} is \emph{re-}, back or anew, plus \textbf{parāre}, to make ready: to make ready once more. The mending sense is already classical — to restore, to put back in order. That much is settled.

How the word reached Spanish is not. Wiktionary tags it inherited from Old Spanish, then adds, in the same entry, that it is possibly a borrowing, and points at Corominas. Two verdicts, one entry.

That is honesty, not sloppiness, and here is why.

A word usually wears its road on its face: \emph{harina} lost an \emph{f} coming down, \emph{noche} turned a Latin cluster into \emph{ch}, and a word copied off a page skipped both. The sounds testify.

Run \emph{reparar} through that test and nothing happens. \emph{Re-} comes out \emph{re-} either way. \emph{Par-} has no cluster to simplify, no \emph{f} to lose, no vowel a sound change could reach. The \emph{-ar} is where Latin \emph{-āre} lands on both roads. No segment would differ by route.

So phonology is silent, and the weight falls entirely on dates and manuscripts. One dictionary can call it inherited and another hedge, neither of them careless. A word can be perfectly well understood and still refuse to say where it has been.

Its commonest modern use is \emph{reparar en} something, to notice it; how the verb travelled from mending to noticing is not accounted for here.

English has two unrelated \textbf{repair}s: the one that mends is \emph{reparāre}; the \emph{repair} of \emph{repair to the drawing room} is Late Latin \emph{repatriāre}, to return to one's country. \textbf{Prepare}, \textbf{apparatus} and \textbf{parade} are true relatives.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name five everyday actions, this one included: \emph{reparar}. And you have met a word whose sounds cannot settle its history.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{reparar}
  \item \emph{reparo el teléfono}
\end{itemize}

Now all five together. Name five everyday actions, and say one thing about each.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{aprender — aprendo en la escuela}
  \item \emph{cocinar — cocino en casa}
  \item \emph{preferir — prefiero el arroz}
  \item \emph{funcionar — el teléfono funciona}
  \item \emph{reparar — reparo la puerta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why can the sounds of \emph{reparar} not settle its history? (No segment of \emph{re-par-ar} would differ on the two roads, so phonology has nothing to give.) And which English \emph{repair} is this word? (The one that mends; the one meaning to betake oneself is \emph{repatriāre}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
